[L17] # UATU DOSSIER — SUBJECT: GRIMM, BENJAMIN JACOB ("THE THING")
[L18] ## SECTION 0 — EXECUTIVE BRIEF (BLUF)

---

[L22] ### Bottom Line Up Front

[L24] Benjamin Jacob Grimm is a man whose entire adult life has been the slow, deliberate, and almost completely successful conversion of catastrophic somatic trauma into protective love. Strip away the rock plates, the Brooklyn cadence, the "Clobberin' Time" branding, the wrestling-circuit detours, the cosmic battle record, the six decades of published incident — and what remains is a poor Jewish kid from Yancy Street who buried his brother before he could shave, who escaped his neighborhood by being useful (football, flight, the Air Force, Reed Richards' rocket), and who has spent the rest of his life trying to remain useful enough to justify the love he cannot quite believe he deserves. That is the through-line. Everything else — the strength, the heroism, the humor, the marriage, the recovered faith — is constructed on top of it.

[L26] He is, on the evidence, **the single most psychologically mature and morally integrated principal subject in the Fantastic Four file, and one of the most stable long-duration superhuman operators on record anywhere.** This assessment is counterintuitive given his presentation (gruff, self-deprecating, visibly damaged) and given the depth of his trauma load (childhood loss, paternal abuse, irreversible somatic catastrophe, repeated near-cures rescinded). It is nonetheless the assessment the evidence requires. The presentation is the disguise; the integration is the fact.

---

[L30] ### Who He Is At The Deepest Level

[L32] At bedrock, Grimm is **a protector who believes he is a monster, operating on the working assumption that the monster's only legitimate use is the protection.** This is the engine. It is not a metaphor — it is a literal operating equation he runs many times a day, in every social interaction, every combat decision, every domestic moment. The equation predates the transformation; the transformation only externalized and confirmed it. The Yancy Street boy who lost his brother already believed, at some pre-verbal level, that he was the wrong one to survive, that his survival was a debt, and that the debt could only be paid in service to the smaller and weaker. The cosmic rays did not create this man. They gave him a body that finally looked, to him, like what he already felt he was.

[L34] He is, secondarily, **a man of pronounced and unadvertised intelligence** — not Richards-grade abstract cognition, but a high-bandwidth social-emotional and kinesthetic intelligence that he actively conceals beneath an anti-pretension brawler's affect. He reads rooms faster than Reed, reads grief faster than Sue, reads adolescent insecurity faster than Johnny, and routinely arrives at the moral conclusion of an episode three beats before the team genius does. He hides this. The hiding is itself diagnostic: he learned early that being the smart one in his family had not saved Daniel, and that being the cautious one on Reed's flight had not saved himself. Cognitive performance, for Ben, is associated with failure-to-prevent. He has accordingly retreated from displaying it.

[L36] He is, thirdly, **a Jew** — and the late-canon reclamation of this identity (the Shema over Sheckerberg; the adult re-affirmed bar mitzvah; the deliberate, public assertion of a faith that predates the lab that broke him) is not ornament. It is the most important single act of self-authorship in his adult life. It locates his moral framework outside the Richards ecosystem, outside the rocket, outside the transformation. It says: *I was someone before this, and I am still someone underneath this, and the someone is older than the cosmic rays.* The faith is the keel.

[L38] He is, fourthly and finally, **a husband, a father, and the de facto uncle of the Richards children** — and these roles are not biographical decoration but the structural achievement of his life. That a man who entered adulthood convinced he was unlovable and exited his first decade post-transformation convinced he was unmarriageable has built and sustained a marriage, raised children, and serves as the emotional safe-harbor for the two most consequential prodigies of the next generation, is the practical proof of integration. Everything theoretical in this file collapses into that fact.

---

[L42] ### The Through-Line Of His Entire Existence

[L44] The through-line is **survivor's debt, paid in protection, performed as gruffness, sanctified by chosen family.** It runs unbroken from approximately age nine — the death of Daniel — to the present. Every era of his life is a variation on the same theme, and the evolution across the eras is one of *refinement of the same gesture*, not change of gesture.

[L46] - **Childhood (Yancy Street):** Survivor of his brother. Inherits Daniel's gang, fails to be Daniel, leaves the neighborhood. The leaving is itself the original sin he will spend decades atoning for via anonymous donations, charity, and the ritualized "harassment" by the gang he tolerates and even invites.
[L47] - **Adolescence / Early Adulthood (football, college, Air Force):** Achievement as escape, achievement as proof-of-worth, achievement as the form the debt-payment takes when the debtor is young and physically gifted. He becomes useful at scale: pilot, officer, the man you want in your cockpit.
[L48] - **The Rocket:** The founding wound. He is right (the shielding is inadequate), he is overruled, and his rightness is punished with the most extreme of the four transformations. The universe confirms, in the most literal possible way, what he has feared since age nine: that he was the wrong one to survive, and now everyone can see it on him.
[L49] - **Early Thing Era (rage, isolation, Alicia):** The debt becomes unpayable in any prior form (he can no longer simply *be useful and pleasant*) and so it must be paid in the only currency now available: standing between things and harm. Alicia stabilizes him not by curing him but by being the one person whose perception cannot indict him.
[L50] - **Mid-Career (DeFalco, Englehart, the wrestling years, the Battleworld choice):** The first sustained experiments in *autonomous* adulthood. Battleworld is the crux: given the choice to be human elsewhere or rock at home, he chooses elsewhere — and then comes home anyway, because the family is the larger gravity. The wrestling circuit is the rehearsal of being-the-Thing as a *profession*, not just a condition. He learns that the body can be a job rather than a sentence.
[L51] - **Late Career (Hickman, Slott, North):** Integration. Marriage. Faith. Children. He becomes the team's *moral* center rather than its blunt instrument. The protection-engine, formerly aimed at strangers and supervillains, has expanded to encompass the smallest and most vulnerable members of his own household, and the gruffness has thinned to a permeable membrane through which his actual tenderness is visible to anyone willing to look.

[L53] Across all five eras the gesture is the same: *I will stand here so that you do not have to.* What changes is who "you" is (the gang, the squadron, the team, the woman, the children, the world) and how openly he is willing to admit the standing.

---

[L57] ### The Core Wound And Its Maintenance

[L59] **The core wound is not the cosmic rays. The core wound is Daniel.**

[L61] This must be stated plainly because the canon and the subject both invite the misreading that the transformation is the originating injury. It is not. The transformation is the *somatic confirmation* of an injury already in place. The originating injury is the death of an older brother whom Ben idolized, in a neighborhood whose violence Ben survived and Daniel did not, in a family that subsequently dissolved (mother to grief, father to alcohol), leaving Ben to be raised by a healer-uncle whose vocation he could not match and whose decency he could not feel he had earned. By age twelve Ben Grimm had the basic architecture he still carries: *the wrong one lived; the living one owes; the owed must be repaid by becoming useful to the smaller.*

[L63] The cosmic-ray transformation then performed three psychological functions, in this order:

[L65] 1. **It confirmed** the pre-existing self-image (monstrous, wrong-one-to-survive, visibly other).
[L66] 2. **It justified** the protection drive at a new and absolute scale (a body that can absorb harm meant for others is the literal apparatus of debt-repayment).
[L67] 3. **It punished** him with a permanent reminder that he had once again been the one who was right (the radiation warning) and that his rightness had once again failed to save the people he loved (Reed, Sue, Johnny were also exposed; the difference is that his body kept the receipt).

[L69] **Maintenance of the wound** is now performed via a small set of recurring mechanisms which together constitute the daily psychological work of being Ben Grimm:

[L71] - **Mirror avoidance** and the broader pattern of refusing to fully inhabit his own image. This is chronic, low-level, and lifelong. He does not photograph himself for pleasure. He does not linger at reflective surfaces. The avoidance is so habitual it has become postural.
[L72] - **Tolerated displacement** via the Yancy Street Gang gag — a self-administered, low-stakes channel through which neighborhood-of-origin guilt and residual self-contempt are externalized in manageable doses. He could end it any time. He does not. It is therapeutic.
[L73] - **Pre-emptive self-deprecation** as conversational opener — the joke that names the monster first so that no one else has to. This both protects him from being named and protects his interlocutors from the awkwardness of pretending not to notice. It is, on net, generous; it is also a continuous low-grade reinforcement of the negative self-image it is meant to defuse.
[L74] - **Reversion-temptation cycles** that periodically reactivate the original choice-trauma (would I be human if I could?), each cycle ending in re-mutation that the canon increasingly attributes to his own psychogenic refusal to remain human. He cannot stay human because being-the-Thing has become the form his debt-payment takes, and to be cured would be to default.
[L75] - **Reed-relationship friction**, periodically lanced and re-bonded. The "you could have cured me" wound is the one piece of unfinished business he carries against the person he loves most outside his marriage, and he keeps it open — not vindictively, but because closing it would mean either forgiving (which requires admitting he is loved despite the body, which is still hard for him) or breaking (which is unthinkable). He maintains it as a managed grievance instead.
[L76] - **Continuous low-grade somatic grief** around Alicia — the touch he cannot fully feel, the intimacy whose limits the canon euphemizes and he privately mourns. This is the daily price and he pays it daily.

[L78] What he does *not* do to maintain the wound is equally diagnostic: he does not drink at it, does not direct it at innocents, does not let it metastasize into cruelty, does not use it to claim victimhood, does not let it interfere with his showing up. The wound is *contained*. That containment is the work of his life.

---

[L82] ### Operational Summary

[L84] **Designation:** Principal, Fantastic Four. Long-duration superhuman operator, sixty-plus years continuous service with brief self-initiated leaves of absence, all voluntarily ended by return.

[L86] **Reliability:** Maximal under trusted command (Richards, or any commander who has earned his read). Will refuse unethical orders without dramatics; simply will not do them. Has never abandoned a teammate in the field. Has abandoned the team *off* the field on multiple documented occasions, always for stated reasons, always with eventual return. The leaves are not desertions; they are regulator releases.

[L88] **Threat-engagement profile:** Telegraphed, ritualized, target-discriminate aggression. The "Clobberin' Time" verbalization is functionally a *de-escalation cue to bystanders and a permission-slip to himself* — it bounds the violence to follow. He does not enjoy cruelty. He does enjoy combat against legitimate targets, in the way a craftsman enjoys the use of well-fitted tools. He will, in peak-threat conditions involving harm to loved ones, deliver controlled lethal-grade force; he comes down from this state rapidly and moves immediately to comfort the harmed party rather than to celebrate the victory.

[L90] **Corruptibility:** None at the value level. Cannot be bought, cannot be flattered, cannot be coerced via personal threat. *Can* be moved via threats to loved ones, but "moved" is the correct word, not "broken" — he will engage on the adversary's terms only insofar as engagement protects the loved one, and will revert to his own moral code the instant the threat is neutralized. Reversion-offers are the single most destabilizing bait in the catalogue and remain so even now; he is practiced, not immune.

[L92] **Solo viability:** Degraded over long durations. His stability is partly relational and depreciates in isolation. The wrestling-circuit and Battleworld periods document this: he can function alone, but the longer he is alone the more the protection-engine has to find substitute objects, and the substitutes are never as stabilizing as the real family.

[L94] **Domestic / family axis:** Husband to Alicia Masters; father (variously: adopted Jo-Venn and N'Kalla; in some continuities biological children with Alicia); functional uncle and emergency-contact-of-first-resort for Franklin and Valeria Richards. These bonds are the most strategically important variables in his file. He is more himself, more regulated, and more dangerous (in the protective sense) when they are present.

[L96] **Faith axis:** Reclaimed Jewish identity, publicly affirmed in adulthood after decades of private practice. Provides a moral framework that operates independently of the Richards rationalist ecosystem and that the file should treat as a *stabilizer of first rank*. Any analysis that omits this dimension misreads him.

[L98] **Vulnerabilities, ranked:** (1) Harm to Alicia. (2) Harm to the children. (3) Reactivation of the Reed-betrayal wound by adversary action. (4) Credible reversion offers. (5) Forced mirror-confrontations and image-illusions. (6) Threats to Yancy Street or its residents. All vulnerabilities are *exploitable for short-term tactical destabilization* and *not exploitable for long-term value capture*. He cannot be turned. He can be hurt.

[L100] **Prognosis:** Excellent. The trajectory across sixty years is monotonic toward integration. The trauma load is enormous and largely metabolized. The defenses are mature and getting more so. The relationships are stable and deepening. Barring catastrophic loss of Alicia or the children — which would constitute a black-swan event whose consequences this file cannot model with confidence — the subject will continue to function at or near the top of his historical baseline indefinitely.

---

[L104] ### The One-Sentence Brief

[L106] A Yancy Street boy who survived his brother and has spent sixty years standing in front of everyone smaller than he is, in a body that finally matches what he has always quietly believed about himself, doing the work anyway, loved by a family he is still privately surprised to have — and that surprise, the fact that he still notices the love and still does not quite believe he has earned it, is the entire reason he is the most trustworthy man in the file.

% IMPERIUS REX: THE TRIAL OF A KING
% An Earth-GK Courtroom Chronicle
% Unofficial original fiction — narration edition

# PROLOGUE — THE WORDS THAT CROSSED AN OCEAN

The first problem with a king was that nobody ever told him to stop talking.

The second problem was that some kings interpreted silence as agreement.

At eleven seventeen on a Thursday morning, Namor McKenzie stood beneath a white canopy on the East River and told the assembled international press that Susan Storm Richards had shared his bed.

He did not whisper it. Kings who intended to whisper things generally found themselves disappointed with the acoustics of their own mouths.

He said it into twenty-six microphones, past the discreetly horrified face of the State Department's maritime liaison, and directly toward a television camera whose red light he had mistaken for the respectful gaze of history.

"Lady Susan has known me as a woman knows a man," he declared. "She has shared my bed. The surface may find this inconvenient. I do not."

A reporter coughed. Another lifted her phone higher. The Atlantean diplomatic party stood very still.

Across Manhattan, in a laboratory on the upper floors of the Baxter Building, Reed Richards was calculating the nonuniform expansion of a ceramic pressure seal when his wife appeared in the doorway.

Reed had been married long enough to know that the absence of sound could itself be a communication.

"Susan," he said, lifting his eyes from the display.

"Did you see it?"

"Yes."

"And?"

He turned his chair all the way toward her, deliberately clearing his hands from the instruments. It was a learned act of attention, not an instinct. She recognized the effort. More importantly, she recognized that it was real.

"I believe," Reed said, "that he has made a statement he cannot substantiate."

Sue watched him for another second. Then she nodded, once.

"Good. Because I am not spending the afternoon proving which bed I was in twenty years ago. I am going to find out why he needed the world to believe it today."

A second screen lit up.

The Department of State had accepted an emergency maritime filing from the Kingdom of Atlantis. The filing named Susan Storm Richards as a consenting Atlantean consort and jointly authorized custodian of a relief corridor extending from the continental shelf to the mouths of three American harbors. It included a document bearing what appeared to be her signature.

Three humanitarian ships had been ordered to hold position outside the corridor pending clarification of competing sovereign authority. The nearest vessel carried refrigeration for transplant organs and dialysis supplies.

Sue read the notice. Her expression did not change.

Reed stood.

"That," she said quietly, "is not my signature."

At the far end of the building, Johnny Storm was replaying the press conference for the fourth time, mouth open in something between delighted horror and a genuine desire to fly directly through a royal yacht.

Ben Grimm entered carrying coffee in two mugs, took one look at the screen, and said, "Kid, don't."

"I haven't done anything."

"You got that look."

"What look?"

"The look where the whole city has to call its insurance company."

Johnny was about to make a joke when Sue walked in. He saw her face and swallowed it.

"We need a lawyer," she said.

Ben set down the mugs.

"A good one?"

"An exceptionally good one."

Johnny blinked. "Okay, but are we talking 'the kind who wins' or 'the kind who can survive Thanksgiving after meeting us'?"

"Both," Sue said.

Three blocks away, in a third-floor office with a permanently unreliable radiator, Matthew Murdock heard a telephone ring and knew, before anybody picked it up, that his afternoon was about to become complicated.

He did not know the details yet.

His body had simply developed a professional response to the sound of trouble approaching with excellent diction.

---

# CHAPTER ONE — NELSON AND MURDOCK

Foggy Nelson was eating soup over a sealed deposition when Matt entered the office carrying no umbrella, despite the steady October rain.

"No," Foggy said.

"I haven't asked you anything."

"You have that face."

"I have one face."

"And yet it manages to invoice me in different currencies. That one costs overtime."

The telephone rang again.

Foggy examined the number and forgot his soup.

"Baxter Building," he said.

Matt extended a hand. Foggy passed him the receiver.

They listened to Sue Richards explain what had happened. She explained it in chronological order, in ordinary language, without adjectives she did not need. A press statement. An alleged consort appointment. An emergency federal filing. Her name. A signature that was not hers. Three delayed ships. A man who had spent years treating the difference between her affection and her consent as a negotiable detail.

When she finished, Matt asked one question.

"What do you want fixed first?"

Sue did not answer immediately. It was the first pause of the call that sounded like surprise.

"The ships," she said. "Before anybody debates my marriage or his dignity, get the ships moving."

"Then that's first."

By one o'clock, the office was full.

There was Sue, in an understated charcoal suit. Reed came with a neat folder of documents and no presentation graphics, having been asked by his wife not to arrive carrying a machine with exposed capacitors. Johnny came because somebody had to be available to turn bad decisions into good distractions. Ben came because Sue had asked him to.

Foggy came out of the back office holding a yellow legal pad.

"Before anybody says the word 'defamation,'" he announced, "I would like to remind the room that there are three ships involved and two different legal problems. We're not putting a guy in federal prison because he told an obnoxious lie about his sex life."

Johnny leaned back. "What if he told it really obnoxiously?"

"Still not a felony."

"I hate law."

"Then stop committing to it in public."

Matt waited until the laughter thinned. "The criminal issue isn't the boast. It's the filing. If somebody knowingly submitted a false material statement to a federal agency, or forged authority to control emergency operations, that can become a federal criminal case. But we're not the prosecutors. We can represent Susan, protect her interests, and supply authenticated evidence. The United States Attorney decides what to charge."

Sue nodded. That was the first lawyer she'd met all morning who hadn't offered to purchase a press release with her own money.

Reed opened the folder.

"The supposed signature was derived from a scan of an actual humanitarian clearance I signed with Susan two years ago. I can demonstrate the shared defect pattern at a resolution sufficient to establish common ancestry."

"Can you establish that it was copied without relying on the fact that you're Reed Richards?" Foggy asked.

Reed looked at him, interested rather than insulted.

"Yes. An independent document examiner can repeat the analysis. The pixel geometry is measurable."

"Good," Foggy said. "Because I love your science, but juries should never have to take a genius's word for anything."

"Agreed," Reed replied.

Sue placed another document on the table. It was a letter she had sent privately to Namor six days earlier.

Its language was civil, precise, and decisive.

She would assist in protecting the trench. She would not serve as Atlantis's consort, regent, or diplomatic proxy. Any memorandum describing her as such would be false. The presence of her name on a rescue agreement required her actual approval, not a presumption based on previous friendship.

"He acknowledged receipt," she said. "Not by messenger. Not through an aide. Personally."

Matt felt the paper between his fingers. He could not inspect printed ink as another lawyer could. He could read its embossed header, and he could listen when Foggy read the rest to him. The distinction mattered. He had spent years fighting the temptation to treat extraordinary senses as permission to skip ordinary proof.

"May we preserve both the original and its transmission record?" he asked.

"Already done," Reed said. "I separated the originals from the working copies and generated independent hashes."

Foggy pointed his pen at Reed. "If you could do that for our copier, I'd start charging you less."

A small sound came from Ben. Not quite a laugh. Ben had been watching Sue.

"Susie," he said, "he's gonna make it about whether you ever wanted him."

"I know."

"And you don't owe a courtroom a tour of your private life."

"I know that too."

"Then you want me there?"

She reached across the table and squeezed the rock-plated hand large enough to cover hers completely.

"Yes. I want somebody in that room who remembers that I get to speak for myself."

Matt sat very still.

He had heard a great many clients ask lawyers to make them innocent. He had heard clients ask to be believed, defended, hidden, rescued, forgiven. Sue Richards was asking him to preserve the distinction between the thing that happened and the story powerful people found useful.

That was a request he understood.

Outside, a siren moved down Tenth Avenue. He could hear the uneven breath of someone running behind it, the roar of a passing delivery truck, and the faint melodic buzz of Foggy's forgotten phone vibrating against its charger.

He let all of it remain background.

"Susan," he said, "I'm going to ask the government to reopen the shipping corridor today. I'll ask for protective handling of your private communications. And if the filing was knowingly false, we'll make sure the investigators get evidence that can survive cross-examination."

Johnny cleared his throat. "And what do I do?"

"Nothing illegal," Matt said.

"Could you be more specific?"

"No property damage. No flying into diplomatic buildings. No threats on social media."

"You're taking all the joy out of this."

Matt smiled. "I'm a Catholic lawyer. We have a reputation to maintain."

For the first time that day, Sue laughed.

It was brief. But everybody in the room heard it.

---

# CHAPTER TWO — THE FOURTH ENVELOPE

At three twenty-five, a State Department lawyer named Eleanor Vale arrived at the Southern District courthouse carrying four envelopes.

The first contained the original Atlantean submission. The second held a federal registry receipt. The third contained an authenticated letter from the Atlantean Council of Eight Cities.

The fourth had been placed in her hand by the deputy secretary himself.

She did not like the fourth envelope. It was the sort of envelope that changed who a government was permitted to pretend had authority.

Across the street, Johnny Storm waited outside the metal detector with a paper cup of coffee, his hands conspicuously empty.

"I'm behaving," he assured the marshal.

"That's usually what people say before I ask them to take their belts off," the marshal replied.

Inside, a line of reporters curved around a marble pillar. Somebody had already printed KING OF ATLANTIS CLAIMS IMMUNITY across an evening-news banner. Another network had chosen FANTASTIC FOUR LOVE TRIANGLE GOES FEDERAL.

Sue walked straight past both.

Matt counted the acoustics: thirty-eight reporters, two television booms, three diplomatic security teams, and a heartbeat near the north doors moving much too quickly for the quiet man attached to it.

He turned slightly toward Foggy.

"The fellow by the blue column. Tell security somebody may have brought a restricted recording device."

Foggy glanced. "How do you know?"

"Metal casing. Electrical whine. He's turning it on and off whenever Vale moves."

"We are not going to make you a witness, Matt."

"Then don't tell them I heard it. Ask them to check their own equipment policy."

Foggy smiled. "There you are. An actual lawyer."

In a windowless conference room, Vale opened the first three envelopes before the prosecutor, Assistant United States Attorney Nora Malik. On the last she rested her palm.

"My office has received a formal request from Mr. McKenzie's counsel for a suggestion of head-of-state immunity."

"And?" Malik asked.

"The United States does not currently recognize him as the sitting sovereign of Atlantis."

"Since when?"

"Eleven weeks."

Malik put her pen down.

Vale opened the fourth envelope. Inside was a copy of the abdication instrument Namor had signed at the emergency session of the Council of Eight Cities. Atlantis had retained its monarchy in ceremonial form, but executive authority had transferred to the council during the rebuilding of the southern trench. The Council's notice had been delivered to the State Department and acknowledged. Namor could still call himself king. He could not claim to exercise the Council's legal powers for the purposes of this agreement.

"It was his signature?" Malik asked.

"Authenticated by the Council. We're providing the record, not asking you to trust our interpretation."

"Why didn't the department release it when he held that press conference?"

Vale gave her a tired look. "Because our job is to answer the question before us, not to provide commentary on the romantic judgment of foreign dignitaries."

Malik almost smiled.

"Does your department intend to recommend immunity anyway?"

"No current-head-of-state immunity. Other objections will be litigated. His counsel knows that."

An hour later, the government asked the judge for an emergency hearing. The filing that had kept the ships offshore was not merely questionable; the person claiming exclusive state authority had no authority under the agreement's own succession clause, and the woman named as cosignatory denied the document.

The relief ships were released pending independent port-security checks.

Matt called Sue from the courthouse steps.

"The first vessel has clearance. The others are moving through ordinary inspection."

He heard her release a breath she had been holding since the laboratory.

"Thank you," she said.

"That's only the shipping issue."

"I know."

"The United States Attorney is opening a criminal investigation into the filing."

"Good."

"That doesn't mean the private boast will be prosecuted."

"Matthew," Sue said, with something almost affectionate in her patience, "I've never once confused the two."

He heard the call end and smiled to himself.

Across the courthouse plaza, the man with the recording device was stopped at security, questioned, and allowed to leave after the device was inspected. It was a high-powered transmitter. Its contents were ordinary press files and a single encrypted burst addressed to a remote server.

The burst had been sent twelve seconds after Vale entered the building.

Matt had no evidence yet that it was criminal.

But he remembered the timing.

He had learned that a small honest observation could be the first loose thread in a very expensive lie.

The story has its legal hinge now: **the sexual boast is not the crime**. The criminal case is built around a knowingly false diplomatic filing that uses Sue’s supposed consent to exercise authority over a maritime relief corridor. That gives Matt a real courtroom problem, Namor a sovereignty defense, the State Department a consequential role, and Sue a reason to take the stand that has nothing to do with proving her virtue.

# CHAPTER THREE — NO CROWN IN THIS COURT

Ten days later, Namor McKenzie entered a federal courtroom as if a judge had requested an audience.

The difference mattered to everyone in the room except him.

He wore a dark suit in place of royal armor, but the effect was nearly the same. There were men who required jewels to suggest royalty. Namor had been crowned young enough to forget that most people had to learn how to stand without being bowed to.

Judge Elena Salcedo looked over her glasses.

"Mr. McKenzie."

"Your Honor."

"I appreciate the restraint of your entrance."

A faint ripple passed through the gallery. It was not quite laughter; no one was prepared to gamble on the judge's definition of contempt this early.

At the defense table, attorney Adrian Kessler rose. He was impeccably calm and professionally brave in the way of people who had agreed to bill a monarch by the hour.

"Your Honor, we renew our motion to dismiss for sovereign immunity. Whatever terminology the Department of State now prefers, my client remains a king under the ancient law of Atlantis."

"Then he may remain one there," Salcedo replied. "My responsibility is to determine whether this court has jurisdiction over the offenses in this indictment. Please proceed with the law, not the biography."

Kessler presented the argument with care. Foreign sovereigns were not ordinary litigants. A state could not adjudicate another nation's legitimacy through a domestic popularity contest. Recognition was a political decision. Diplomatic communications were official acts. No American judge should casually substitute a courtroom finding for an executive determination.

It was a serious argument, which was why Salcedo listened to it seriously.

Malik stood when invited. She presented the government record: the current recognition notice, the Council of Eight Cities' transfer instrument, and the narrower character of the charges.

"The government is not prosecuting a policy decision of Atlantis," she said. "Count One alleges that Mr. McKenzie knowingly submitted a materially false statement to the United States Department of State. Count Two alleges an agreement with a second individual to impair the Department's lawful administration of the maritime relief program. We will have to prove those allegations. We are not asking this court to decide whether he deserves a throne."

The judge turned toward Namor.

"Sir, you may understand yourself to remain king. That self-understanding isn't evidence of the immunity you assert. The State Department confirms that the United States does not presently recognize you as the sitting holder of Atlantis's executive office. The motion is denied on the record and arguments currently before me. You may preserve the question for appeal."

Namor's jaw tightened. For a moment Matt heard the small, dangerous adjustment of weight that preceded many fights.

Kessler placed two fingers on the edge of his client's sleeve.

Namor did not move.

"We now turn," Salcedo said, "to a much less interesting question than royal honor. What was actually submitted to the government?"

The jury was selected over the next two days. There were twelve jurors: a nurse, a retired machinist, a grocery manager, a software tester, two office workers, a teacher, a transit mechanic, a postal supervisor, an accountant, a line cook, and a woman whose answer to the judge's question about superheroes was, "I have no idea why any of them think they can park wherever they want."

Johnny liked that juror immediately.

"We should adopt her," he whispered.

"You're already enough trouble," Ben whispered back.

Matt did not sit at the government's table. He sat with Foggy on the victims' counsel side of the gallery, a position that gave him neither the prosecutor's authority nor a license to interfere. He represented Sue. Malik represented the United States. They shared evidence when lawful and disagreed when necessary.

Sue had chosen not to attend jury selection. She had spent those two days at the harbor, checking the resupply operation she had been falsely certified to control.

When opening statements began, she was in the second row. Reed sat beside her, his hands folded in an arrangement too deliberate to be comfortable. Ben sat on the aisle. Johnny leaned forward so far he seemed to be negotiating with gravity.

Malik opened with the filing.

"Ladies and gentlemen, you have heard a great deal outside this room about whether the defendant was loved. That is not your question. This is a case about what he knew when he told the United States that another person had agreed to act for his government. A federal agency relied on that representation. Emergency shipping was delayed. We will prove that the signature was forged and that the defendant knew the represented consent had been refused before he signed."

Kessler's opening was leaner.

"My client signed what his court assured him was a genuine diplomatic authorization. He is proud, difficult, and capable of a spectacularly unwise public statement. None of those characteristics is a crime. The government will ask you to infer knowledge from embarrassment. The law requires proof."

Matt liked Kessler less with every sentence for the deeply inconvenient reason that Kessler was doing his job well.

The judge instructed the jury to consider the evidence and not the audience.

"No witness's stature will make a fact true," she said, "and no defendant's unpopularity will make it false."

Namor watched her.

It was the first statement that morning he appeared to take personally.

---

# CHAPTER FOUR — DOOM DOES NOT SWEAR TWICE

Victor von Doom arrived without an entourage.

That was more alarming than if he had arrived with an army.

He entered the court through a side door negotiated in advance by the marshals and the State Department. His green cloak barely moved. The metal of his mask caught the overhead lights without reflecting much of anything at all.

There were three sounds in the room: fabric sliding against armor, a juror drawing in a breath, and the soft, involuntary sigh of Reed Richards discovering that the day's plans had survived him only in outline.

"Victor," Reed said.

"Richards."

Sue looked at Doom. He inclined his head to her, formally.

"Susan."

"Victor."

Johnny leaned toward Ben. "Is this the part where the ceiling falls in?"

"If it is," Ben said, "I'm billing you for the roof."

Doom was called not to discuss bedrooms but to authenticate the transfer of executive authority. The Council of Eight Cities had convened part of its emergency session under Latverian neutral-host protocols. Doom had witnessed the final instrument and bound his own office to retain an authenticated record.

Kessler objected to the dramatic potential of the witness before he objected to the evidence.

Judge Salcedo ignored the first problem and addressed the second.

"Dr. von Doom, are you prepared to take an oath to tell the truth?"

"Doom has sworn to preserve the integrity of this instrument."

"That wasn't my question."

The entire courtroom became quieter.

Doom regarded the judge. She regarded him back.

"Yes," he said at last.

"Thank you. The clerk will administer the oath."

Matt heard Johnny's suppressed laugh shake the bench.

Malik began with the ordinary foundations. Had Doom attended? Yes. Had he seen Namor sign? Yes. Had the transfer been effective on the date stated? Yes. Did the version presented to the Department of State match the instrument he had witnessed? The authentication marks, he explained, were identical. Two independent experts from the Court's own staff had already confirmed the ordinary physical and digital features; his testimony supplied the eyewitness chain.

"Why," Malik asked, "did your government retain an original?"

"Because sovereignty is too important to entrust to the memory of courtiers."

"And what authority did Mr. McKenzie retain?"

"He retained his title, ceremonial duties, and a voice before the Council. He relinquished executive control of the southern trench restoration and treaty submissions pertaining to it."

Kessler rose to cross-examine.

"Dr. von Doom, you have a history of rivalry with Mr. McKenzie, don't you?"

"You will have to specify which war."

A juror covered her mouth.

"You would benefit from seeing Atlantis weakened."

"Latveria benefits from stable borders and reliable signatures. Atlantis weakened by a childish forgery would be a nuisance, not an advantage."

"You dislike my client's manner."

"I dislike many manners. I have not brought them all before a tribunal."

"And your interest here is purely civic?"

Doom turned his mask toward Namor. For once he seemed to forget the lawyers.

"The man gave his word. I witnessed it. If a sovereign wishes to reclaim surrendered authority, he must seek it through law or force. He may not have it by pretending a woman signed what she did not sign."

Kessler paused.

"Are you saying Mr. McKenzie forged the signature?"

"No," Doom said. "I am saying what I have personally observed. A distinction a competent attorney should appreciate."

Matt lowered his head. Foggy could tell from the angle that he was smiling.

"Your Honor," Kessler said, "I ask that the last comment be stricken."

"The witness's evaluation of counsel will be disregarded," Salcedo said. "The factual testimony stands."

Doom stepped down.

Passing Sue's row, he stopped and held her gaze a fraction longer than etiquette required.

"You are under no obligation to thank me," he said.

"I wasn't going to," Sue replied.

Something about Doom's posture changed. It was only an infinitesimal lift of the chin, but Reed recognized it as the Victor equivalent of a delighted smile.

"Excellent," Doom said, and left.

Outside, reporters converged on the exit. Doom passed through them with the effortless indifference of a man who had long ago outsourced public opinion to history.

Inside, Malik's next witness entered with a document case.

And at the defense table, Namor finally looked less angry than uncertain.

---

# CHAPTER FIVE — A SIGNATURE HAS A SHADOW

A forged signature was an unusually personal kind of lie. It did not merely put words in somebody's mouth. It borrowed their hand.

That, Reed thought, was why Sue had been so quiet about it.

The government's document examiner, Dr. Celia Park, described the evidence without theatricality. The attestation contained a signature image ostensibly made by Susan Storm Richards. The mark matched an earlier signed humanitarian notice, including an irregular dot just beneath the second stroke of the R in Richards. In genuine separate handwritten signatures, Park explained, natural variations accumulated. In the two records before the court, the imperfections matched point for point.

"Could two human signatures be that alike?" Malik asked.

"Not at the resolution and across the mechanical features we're discussing. My conclusion is that one was derived from an image of the other."

"Can you tell who copied it?"

"No."

"Can you tell us who authorized the use?"

"No."

"Thank you."

Reed observed from the witness bench an hour later as a separate technical witness. He was asked to explain how the Baxter Foundation's emergency seal worked. He began with the physics, then stopped when the judge interrupted.

"Dr. Richards, in plain language, please."

He considered the request carefully.

"The system records when a person actually approves a request. The record includes a sequence number generated by an independent device that the file's author cannot predict in advance. You can copy a picture of a signature. You cannot make a copied picture generate an earlier sequence number from a device that wasn't present."

"You mean this document claimed an event that didn't happen?" Malik asked.

"The evidence establishes that the depicted approval event did not occur in the registered system. It does not establish who made the false claim."

Malik nodded. She had learned not to ask Reed for an answer broader than the data.

On cross-examination, Kessler suggested the instrument might have failed under unusual electromagnetic conditions. Reed conceded that sensors could fail. He was then asked how he could be certain this wasn't the case here.

"Because the independent devices did record the signing of the original humanitarian notice, and they recorded ordinary activity at the time this later approval was said to occur. There is no missing interval. The later filing presents a record of an approval the system never made."

"But the system was built by your laboratory."

"Yes."

"And you are the complaining witness's husband."

"Yes."

"So you have every reason to want to prove her innocent."

Reed tilted his head.

"Mr. Kessler, she's not accused of a crime."

For a moment the exchange was so stark the court could not tell whether it was a rebuke or a correction. It was both.

"You want to vindicate her account," Kessler tried again.

"I want the evidence to be accurate. If it showed her authentic approval, I would have to tell her so, however unpleasant the consequences. I cannot improve my marriage by falsifying an instrument."

In the gallery Sue looked at him. The affection in her expression was unshowy and unembarrassed.

Matt heard the change in her breathing. He did not pretend it was evidence. He was simply glad for them.

By late afternoon Malik had introduced the federal receipt confirming that the document had been transmitted from an Atlantean diplomatic office. The sender account belonged to the acting chief of royal archives, Kheled Voss. The attached certification bore Namor McKenzie's signature and a typed declaration that he had personally verified Susan Richards's acceptance.

The defense stipulated that Namor had signed the page. It did not stipulate that he knew Voss's underlying documentation was false.

That distinction was the case.

At five, as the jury was dismissed, Foggy received a message from a port-security officer. The high-powered transmitter stopped at the courthouse ten days earlier was registered to a contractor hired by the Atlantean diplomatic mission. Its encrypted traffic could not be opened without process, but the registration logs and timing records had been preserved.

Matt wanted to chase the connection. His body wanted to be in motion long before his conscience had finished evaluating the lawful options.

Foggy read his face.

"No rooftops," he said.

"I'm not going onto any rooftops."

"You thought it."

"I was considering the logistical advantages."

"We're getting a subpoena. Let Malik do her job."

Matt exhaled through his nose. "You're right."

"That must have hurt."

"Don't get accustomed to it."

They walked out into an evening cold enough to bring the harbor's salt smell all the way up the avenues. Across the water, two ships moved slowly toward the city, their running lights shining through the haze.

The third was still undergoing inspection.

Matt watched the light he could not see by listening to the engines that carried it.

The ships were moving. The law, perhaps, was moving with them.

---

# CHAPTER SIX — THE MAN FROM WAKANDA

T'Challa did not enter the courthouse as a celebrity.

He entered as a head of state who understood that public restraint was often the most effective form of power.

There was no vibranium suit in view. No theatrical escort. Only dark clothing, a small Wakandan security detail, and the composure of a man whose government had survived enough international negotiations to recognize a poor one before it began.

Johnny watched him pass.

"Well," he whispered, "there goes every joke I prepared."

"A national tragedy," Ben murmured.

The prosecutor had called T'Challa for one precise reason. He had been present when the maritime agreement was discussed. He could testify to the emergency relief arrangements, to the limits of Namor's authority under the council transition, and to a private exchange held in a room containing three diplomats and a recording clerk.

He could not testify to Susan Storm's private history. He said so before anybody asked.

Malik established that Wakanda had offered emergency desalination units and medical transport for civilians along the affected coastal shelf. The relief passage required mutual consent between port authorities and the Atlantean Council. A private person could join the effort as a humanitarian observer, but could not acquire state power by implication.

"Did Mr. McKenzie discuss Susan Richards's role with you?" Malik asked.

"Yes. He said she would stand with him."

"What did you understand that to mean?"

"I asked him."

"What did he say?"

"That she would be recognized as his consort, and that her endorsement would resolve the question of Baxter Foundation participation."

"What did you tell him?"

"That Susan Richards would have to answer for Susan Richards."

The testimony was unspectacular. It was also devastating in the way accurate statements often are when everybody else has been performing.

On cross-examination, Kessler asked whether T'Challa had seen the purported signature before Namor submitted it.

"No."

"Did Mr. McKenzie show you a forged document?"

"No."

"Did he state, in your presence, that he knew the document was false?"

"No."

"Then you cannot tell this jury what he knew."

"I can tell them what he was told," T'Challa replied. "I told him that Susan must agree for herself. Whether he listened is for you to establish."

Kessler pressed once more. "You're also a friend of the Richards family."

"I have worked with them."

"And you are no admirer of my client."

T'Challa gave a slight inclination of his head.

"I have admired him when he earned it. You will find that harder to characterize as bias."

When he stepped down, he passed Sue and paused just long enough to acknowledge her.

"Your ships?" he asked.

"Two cleared. One more this evening."

"Good."

They did not discuss the press conference. They did not discuss Namor's boast. The absence of those subjects was not avoidance. It was respect.

Outside the courthouse, Johnny was surrounded by microphones.

"Mr. Storm, do you have a comment on the allegation that your sister—"

"Yes," Johnny said. "I do. The allegations about her bedroom have dominated your questions while people have been waiting for medical equipment to clear a harbor. Try putting that on your front page."

The reporters looked disappointed. They had expected an explosion. He gave them an accounting.

Back inside, Sue waited for him near the elevator.

"I heard what you said."

Johnny shrugged. "I couldn't think of anything funny."

"I know."

"You okay?"

Sue looked at her brother for a moment. Behind the expensive jacket, the perfect teeth, and the practiced performance of effortless good humor, she could still see the boy who had once followed her through rooms that were far too quiet.

"Not entirely," she said.

That answer was important. She had spent a lifetime saying she was fine when she meant that she intended to remain functional.

Johnny reached out. His hand hovered before resting gently against her shoulder.

"I'll walk you upstairs," he said.

"Thank you."

They walked together.

For once, neither of them felt compelled to make a joke.

# CHAPTER SEVEN — THE MAN WHO BORROWED A QUEEN

Kheled Voss wore the dark blue ceremonial collar of the Atlantean archive service. The collar was old. The man inside it looked tired enough to have spent the last week thinking very hard about his next ten years.

He entered under a limited cooperation agreement. He had not been promised immunity. He had agreed to testify truthfully about his own conduct and the records he handled, knowing that he might be charged separately.

Malik established the system first: a restricted diplomatic relay, a document repository, a signature archive, and an outgoing attestation that had traveled through the archive office before arriving in Washington.

"Did you create the disputed signature image?" she asked.

"Yes."

There was no movement from Sue. There was no movement from Reed. Johnny shifted in his seat and then forced himself to stay still.

"How?"

"The office had access to previous humanitarian correspondence. I used the image from a legitimate letter and placed it on the new instrument."

"Did Susan Richards authorize that?"

"No."

"Why did you do it?"

Voss looked toward Namor, then down again.

"I believed the Council had weakened Atlantis. The emergency corridor would give the Council control of equipment and access that belonged to the throne. If Lady Susan's name appeared beside the king's, the surface governments would accept the transition as a formality."

"You were trying to restore the powers he had surrendered?"

"Yes."

"Did Mr. McKenzie order you to counterfeit her signature?"

The question rested in the room.

"Not in those words," Voss said.

"What words?"

"He told me she had refused the office. He said the Council could not be allowed to use her refusal as an excuse to surrender the corridor to surface contractors. He told me to bring him a completed instrument."

Kessler was on his feet.

"Objection. The witness is characterizing statements without adequate foundation for the date and communication."

Salcedo asked Malik to establish the date and means. Voss identified the conversation, the office, and a contemporaneous relay entry. The judge permitted the testimony subject to cross-examination.

Kessler approached the lectern with a thin smile.

"Mr. Voss, you forged the signature."

"Yes."

"You controlled the office account."

"Yes."

"You hoped to restore the political influence of an office that employed you."

"Yes."

"And now you would very much like this jury to believe you were merely acting under somebody else's instructions."

"I have not said that."

"You say my client told you to bring him a completed instrument. He didn't tell you to forge one."

"He did not use that word."

"You chose the illegal method."

"Yes."

Kessler turned toward the jury.

"No further questions."

That should have been the end of the afternoon.

It was not.

The government's next witness, a federal records custodian, testified that the courthouse transmitter was part of a remote document-wipe system registered to a contractor who maintained Voss's office archives. The burst sent on the day of the immunity hearing triggered a deletion request on a U.S.-based backup server. The server's ordinary retention system had preserved the request and the documents it had attempted to remove.

Malik introduced the relevant extract. It included a record of Voss telling Namor that Sue's written refusal had arrived and that the consent document should be withdrawn. A response from the royal device had followed less than an hour later.

The response said only: Proceed. I will take responsibility.

The defense challenged whether Voss might have generated the message himself. The custodian could establish the relay path and device identity, but not the identity of the fingers that pressed send. A palace communications officer could account for the device's ordinary custody. The government had not yet established that no one else had used it that evening.

The judge admitted the record for the limited purpose for which it had been authenticated, and warned the jurors not to jump from a device to a person without weighing the other testimony.

Matt was grateful for the instruction. Even a man who could hear a room breathe could not know everything that had happened in a room he hadn't entered.

After court adjourned, Sue stood by an empty hallway window. Below her, the street had become a river of camera lights.

"He knew," she said.

"The evidence is pointing there," Matt replied. "But the defense has a fair question about the device."

"He received my letter. He answered it. And he signed anyway."

"That's stronger than any opinion we have about his character. Your testimony matters."

She looked away.

"Do you know what everyone is going to ask me?"

"Yes."

"They'll ask about kisses. About years. They'll ask how I felt when he looked at me. They'll want a map of my marriage."

"Not if I can prevent questions that have no legitimate purpose."

"Can you?"

"I can ask the judge to enforce relevance and protect you from harassment. I can't promise the defense won't test the communications or the relationship you had with him. They have a right to challenge the government's theory. But they don't have a right to turn your testimony into a referendum on whether you were a good wife."

"Good," she said.

For a moment she rested her forehead against the cool glass.

"Matthew, there were times when Namor made me feel seen. That is true. It wasn't charity. It wasn't a trick. There were times I wanted to be somewhere people did not ask me to carry every wall in the house."

Matt waited.

"But I didn't choose Atlantis. And I didn't give him the right to tell the world that I did."

"Then that's what we'll protect," he said.

She straightened.

Through the window, a massive figure in an orange overcoat could be seen moving photographers away from the sidewalk so a woman with a stroller could pass.

Ben Grimm, performing crowd control without anybody telling him it was crowd control.

Sue smiled despite herself.

"He always does that," she said.

"What?"

"Makes enough room for somebody else."

---

# CHAPTER EIGHT — THE INVISIBLE WOMAN TAKES THE STAND

Before Sue testified, Matt Murdock argued for the narrowest kind of justice: permission for a witness to keep what the government had not made relevant.

He stood at a pretrial conference with Foggy beside him and asked for a protective ruling under the federal evidence rules. The government's case alleged a false official representation of consent. The defense had latitude to explore communications, motives, access, and prior dealings. It did not have unlimited latitude to question a witness about private sexual history simply because a defendant had made it famous.

Kessler argued that the relationship mattered to his client's belief that consent was forthcoming.

"Belief in future cooperation can be relevant," Matt said. "So can the private communications that contradicted it. A decades-old kiss is not permission to certify a government office in 2026. You don't get to convert gossip into proof by repeating it in a courtroom."

Salcedo allowed inquiry into the relationship only so far as necessary to test the claimed basis for Namor's belief and knowledge. She barred inflammatory questions with no substantial probative value. She warned both sides against using a person's private conduct as an argument about moral worth.

"This witness," she said, "is not on trial. The indictment specifies what is."

When Sue took the stand, the room seemed to shrink around her.

It was not because she had used her powers. She had used none. She wore an ordinary navy suit, a simple wedding ring, and an expression people who had underestimated her had been learning to fear for sixty years.

Malik began gently.

"Please state your name for the record."

"Susan Storm Richards."

"Did you agree to serve as an Atlantean consort or regent?"

"No."

"Did you sign the document admitted as Government Exhibit Twelve?"

"No."

"Did you authorize anyone to attach your signature to it?"

"No."

"Did you tell the defendant that you would not accept that office?"

"Yes. In writing and before that, face to face."

"Why did you write the letter?"

"Because he kept speaking as if my answer was part of a negotiation I hadn't agreed to have. I wanted there to be no ambiguity. I wanted the people organizing medical relief to be able to trust what I was actually offering."

"What were you offering?"

"Engineering support. Protection for civilians. My own time. Not ownership of my name."

The prosecutor introduced the letter and its authenticated receipt. Sue explained that Namor responded personally, acknowledging that she would provide assistance in her own capacity. She confirmed that the response contained no promise from her to reconsider the consort position.

Kessler stood.

He did not take the bait of the press coverage. He asked first about years of friendship, joint diplomatic work, occasions on which Sue had trusted Namor's help to protect civilians. Sue answered accurately.

"You have sometimes been emotionally close to him?"

"Yes."

"You have kissed him?"

"Yes."

A soft electric disturbance passed through the gallery as reporters leaned forward.

Sue did not look toward them.

"And you understood that he loved you?" Kessler asked.

"I understood that he said he did. I also understood that he loved Atlantis, his crown, and the version of himself he saw when someone admired him. Those things were not always easy to separate."

"Isn't it possible that he believed you would eventually agree to his proposal?"

"It's possible he wanted to believe that."

"But you cannot know what he believed."

"No. I can tell you what I told him."

Kessler moved a little closer.

"Mrs. Richards, the statement he made to the press—"

Malik objected to the proposed line. Matt had not moved, but his hand rested on the edge of the approved protective order. Salcedo required Kessler to state his purpose.

"To establish whether there was a personal intimacy that could inform his understanding of her position."

The judge allowed the narrow question, but not speculation about sexual detail or the marital implications of the answer.

Kessler returned to Sue.

"Was his public statement that you shared his bed true?"

"No."

He seemed momentarily surprised by the simplicity of it.

"You are telling this court you never had sexual intercourse with Namor McKenzie?"

"That is correct."

"Despite your admitted romantic feelings?"

"Counsel," she said, "wanting somebody's attention is not the same as giving that person your consent. You can be attracted to a man, care for him, even kiss him, and still refuse him. Those aren't contradictions."

Kessler drew breath.

"And despite what was happening in your marriage—"

"Objection," Malik said.

"Sustained," Salcedo replied. "We've established the scope of this testimony."

Sue waited until the lawyer looked back at her.

"For the record," she said, before anyone could stop her, "my marriage is not a defense the defendant can borrow. I don't have to prove I was a perfect wife to prove I didn't sign his form."

The judge allowed the answer to stand, as it responded to the direction of the permitted question. Then she reminded everyone to keep to the material issues.

There was no applause. There were no speeches. In a real courtroom, vindication often arrived as a clerk marking the next exhibit.

But Ben Grimm looked down at his enormous hands, and Johnny Storm shut his eyes briefly, and Reed Richards made himself stay in his seat when every impulse told him to go to his wife and hold her.

After cross-examination, Malik asked one final question on redirect.

"Mrs. Richards, do you believe your humanitarian cooperation could ever have been mistaken for consent to an official appointment?"

Sue considered the answer rather than reaching for an easy one.

"People can misunderstand each other," she said. "That's why I wrote the letter. After that, misunderstanding required somebody to stop listening."

The judge thanked her.

Sue descended from the stand under her own power, needing no rescue from any of the men who loved her.

At the door of the courtroom, however, she allowed Ben Grimm to offer an arm.

Sometimes independence meant choosing who walked beside you.

---

# CHAPTER NINE — THE KING'S OWN VOICE

Defense counsel did not want Namor to testify.

There were several sensible reasons for this. The first was that the prosecution still bore the burden of proof. The second was that Namor had spent a career confusing sincerity with the right to make declarations. The third was that, while Kessler could control a question, he could not control a monarch who believed silence to be beneath his office.

Namor listened to all three reasons and chose to testify anyway.

"It is your right," Kessler told him. "It is not my recommendation."

"Your recommendation is understood."

"It would mean more to me if you sounded as if it had changed anything."

At the witness stand, Namor accepted the oath. He spoke first of the trench catastrophe and the lives threatened by underwater instability. He described the Council's abdication agreement as a concession he had made to preserve his people's unity. He spoke of polluted currents, damaged fisheries, and surface contractors whose assurances about environmental safety sounded very much like sales language to a nation accustomed to paying for promises made above the waves.

Some of his testimony was compelling. The threat to Atlantean communities was real. The relief mission had been necessary. The Council's interests were not imaginary. Pride and genuine concern could occupy the same man.

Kessler asked whether he had personally created the counterfeit image.

"No."

"Did you instruct Mr. Voss to steal Mrs. Richards's signature?"

"No."

"Did you expect her to help the relief operation?"

"Yes."

"And did you believe the submission would secure the cooperation required to protect your people?"

"Yes."

Kessler sat. There had been no denial of the boast, no explanation of the letter, and no attempt to resolve the central question. It was a carefully drawn line of testimony, not a completed portrait.

Malik approached with a single sheet.

"Mr. McKenzie, did you receive Susan Richards's letter before signing the attestation?"

"Yes."

"Did you read it?"

"Yes."

"Did it say she would accept the position of consort?"

"No."

"Did it say she would be a regent?"

"No."

"Did it authorize you to speak on her behalf?"

"No."

The courtroom was absolutely quiet. Even Johnny's shallow breathing had stopped.

Malik turned the sheet around for the witness.

"And after reading that letter, you signed this declaration: 'I have personally verified Susan Storm Richards's consent to the attached appointment.' Correct?"

"Correct."

"Was that statement true?"

Namor stared at the document as though it were an enemy who had refused to die.

"No."

The sound that followed was not a gasp. It was the collective, involuntary adjustment of twelve human beings discovering that a case had finally become simple.

"Why did you sign it?" Malik asked.

"Because the corridor was going to be taken from Atlantis."

"That wasn't my question."

The prosecutor's voice was neither loud nor cruel.

"Why did you tell the United States you had personally verified consent you knew you did not have?"

The king looked toward Sue. She watched him, neither merciful nor hostile. The look offered him nothing he could use as an excuse.

"Because I thought the truth could wait until after I had forced the world to do the necessary thing."

"And the statement you made at the press conference?"

Kessler rose. "Objection. Beyond the charges, Your Honor."

Malik replied that the public boast had been offered by the defense as context for the defendant's belief and was relevant to credibility after his own testimony. Salcedo permitted a limited inquiry. She would not allow the press conference to become a substitute for the charged acts.

"Was it true that Susan Storm shared your bed?" Malik asked.

Namor's voice dropped.

"No."

"Why did you say it?"

He hesitated for so long Matt heard the blood moving at the base of his throat.

That sound did not tell Matt whether he was honest. A man could be afraid while telling the truth. A man could tell a lie with a steady pulse. Matt had long ago learned that sensing a body was not the same as possessing a soul.

"I wished," Namor said, "to wound the man she chose."

Reed did not react.

"And I wished," Namor continued, each word emerging as if from deep water, "for people to believe I had been chosen instead."

Malik waited.

"You wanted the appearance of consent."

"Yes."

"And you knew the actual answer was no."

"Yes."

No one moved.

He straightened. For an instant a familiar flash of royal fury returned, but there was nowhere useful for it to go.

"I am not afraid of your verdict," he said.

Salcedo leaned forward.

"Mr. McKenzie, whether you fear this court is not before the jury. Kindly answer the questions presented."

Namor looked at her.

"Understood."

Kessler's redirect was brief. Did Namor understand the legal consequences of submitting the filing? Not fully. Had he directed Voss's deletion attempt? No. Had he authorized any computer intrusion, evidence destruction, or witness intimidation? No. Had he sought a personal monetary benefit? No. Was the concern for Atlantean civilians genuine? Yes.

The prosecution did not contradict all of those answers. It did not have to.

The burden remained on it to prove each charged offense, one at a time.

When the witness stepped down, Sue did not look at him.

Her eyes were on the jury.

For the first time in weeks, the case was no longer being decided by the volume of a man's desire.

It was being decided by evidence.

# INTERLUDE — THE THIRD SHIP

The third ship did not clear inspection.

It cleared the paperwork. Then it encountered a reef that wasn't supposed to be there.

The vessel was called the *Mercy Lane*, a small, hard-working medical freighter chartered by people who had already spent too much money trying to save lives no one would remember by name. Its hold contained refrigerated medication, portable dialysis equipment, and a team of nurses who had taken turns sleeping against a bulkhead for forty-eight hours.

The reef appeared on sonar as a sudden vertical line beneath the bow. The captain ordered reverse thrust. The starboard engine stalled. A wave struck from the north. An automated Atlantean exclusion buoy, left active after an earlier survey, began transmitting conflicting navigational warnings.

The bridge officer sent a distress call using words the Coast Guard would recognize and not a single word that would make a good headline.

At the Baxter Building, Reed heard the alert and stood before Sue had finished opening it.

"We can stabilize the vessel from the west," he said. "The wave period is shorter than the ship's righting response."

Sue looked at the chart. "Which side has the patients?"

"The portable dialysis stations are in the forward hold. The refrigeration is aft."

"Then I'll keep the forward compartment level. You handle the hull stresses. Johnny, no open flame near the oxygen cylinders."

Johnny saluted with two fingers. "You always take the fun out of disaster response."

"Yes," she said. "It's a character flaw."

Ben was already headed for the lift.

They reached the waterfront in minutes. Coast Guard cutters were on scene, coordinating with the vessel's captain. A rescue swimmer waved the family toward a gap in the breakwater and pointed at the *Mercy Lane*. The bow was lifting into an unnatural angle. A mast antenna flashed emergency red.

Sue rose into the air above the ship and extended her arms.

The field began as a transparent plate beneath the forward hull, then curved along the keel like a second skin. She adjusted pressure continuously, allowing the ship to roll just enough that the strain would spread instead of snapping the steel.

Reed stretched from the cutter to the freighter, fastening a temporary brace where the starboard supports had begun to buckle. The work was ugly, difficult, and mechanical. It required knowing which part of a system could be forced without breaking the next part. He had always liked that kind of problem.

"Captain," he called, "you have thirty seconds of added stability. Give the engines a cold restart and bring her two points to port."

The captain didn't ask whether the man giving the instruction was famous. She checked the gauges, repeated the command, and did the job.

Johnny flew ahead of the bow with his flame turned down to a narrow white glow, guiding the cutter through the nearest safe water. He kept his body far enough from the medical oxygen and fuel vapor that neither could become part of his heroism.

Ben stood on the rescue cutter's deck with both hands around a mooring line, taking the tension into his own body while the line's metal cleat shrieked. There were easier ways to get injured than this, but not many that made him feel so reliably useful.

"Hey, Stretch," he grunted. "Tell your wife she's doing the heavy lifting. Again."

"I know," Reed replied.

"Just checking."

Belowdecks, a nurse named Pilar Ortega kept one hand on a patient's shoulder and the other on a storage latch, counting aloud so the frightened young technician beside her could match her rhythm. The technician had never seen a force field hold up a freighter. He had, however, seen Nurse Ortega keep calm in a crisis. He decided to trust the second fact.

The ship rocked once more.

Sue caught it.

The strain registered in her shoulders and the deep muscles across her back. She let the field flex, corrected the pressure, and refused to turn it into an unnecessary demonstration of power. The ship needed stability, not spectacle.

Within eleven minutes the *Mercy Lane* was moving under escort into the safe channel. The dialysis supplies remained secure. The medical team reported no new critical injuries. Port safety officers began the ordinary, painstaking process of deciding which cargo could be unloaded first.

Johnny landed beside Sue, whose boots had just reached the pier.

"Can I say it now?"

"Say what?"

"That you were incredible."

"You can say the captain and crew were incredible."

"Can I say both?"

She considered him. "Yes."

He grinned.

An Atlantean liaison approached carrying an urgent message from the courthouse. The press had learned about the rescue and wanted to know whether it proved Sue had accepted the consort position after all. A reporter had already called it a royal reconciliation.

Sue read the message, handed it back, and replied in a voice the liaison would be able to quote without misunderstanding.

"I just helped a ship," she said. "I did not marry a country."

Back in Manhattan, a judge would soon instruct twelve jurors not to treat the rescue as evidence of the defendant's knowledge. The difference between a good act and a legally relevant fact was important.

Sue knew that better than anyone.

For her, the rescue wasn't a statement about Namor, the crown, or the public argument over her body.

It was simply the work.

And the people on the ship were alive to go home.

# CHAPTER TEN — THE ARGUMENT YOU CAN PROVE

When the evidence closed, the lawyers found themselves with a smaller case than the newspapers had promised.

There was no trial of the Fantastic Four's marriage. No criminal charge for making a false romantic boast. No adjudication of whether the King of Atlantis was a good person, a good ruler, or a good lover. The judge had spent two weeks refusing to let the case become any of those things.

There remained a signed federal submission, a written refusal, an authenticated sequence of communications, and the testimony of the man who signed the document.

Malik's closing took twenty-three minutes.

She spoke of the real relief effort, because the relief was why the false statement mattered. She spoke of the Council's transition, because the filing had claimed an authority no individual possessed. She spoke of Voss's forgery, but separated it from the defendant's personal knowledge. She conceded that the government had not proved who pressed every key in the palace, and that the jury could reach different conclusions on the two counts.

"You do not need to decide whether the defendant loved Susan Richards," she told them. "You do not need to decide what you think of kings. You need to decide whether the defendant knowingly told a federal agency that he'd verified a woman's consent when he knew she had said no. He testified that he did. You heard him. Judge his statement by the same standard you would apply to anyone else."

Kessler's closing was careful and, Matt thought, honorable in its way.

He reminded the jurors that Voss had forged the signature without a direct instruction to forge it. He reminded them that a man could commit one wrong without being guilty of every wrong committed in its wake. The government's case against Voss was not a substitute for proof of a conspiracy involving Namor. Kessler did not attempt to erase his client's admission. Instead, he asked that it be confined to what the words and the law supported.

"The prosecution is entitled to your attention," he said. "It is not entitled to more than its evidence proves."

He sat down beside Namor, looking for once like a lawyer who had accepted the case he actually had instead of the one he had hoped to win.

Judge Salcedo instructed the jury on materiality, knowledge, intent, and the separate requirement of an agreement for a conspiracy. She emphasized that a defendant's choice to testify did not change the burden. She warned against deciding the case out of sympathy for Sue, resentment toward Namor, admiration for Reed, or fear of Doom.

Johnny whispered, "Fear of Doom is usually a pretty solid survival strategy."

Ben put one immense finger against his lips.

"We now ask the jury to deliberate," Salcedo said.

They left by the side door.

In the waiting room, Sue drank tea that had gone cold, listening to Reed explain a technical problem until he reached the end of his own sentence and stopped himself.

"You're doing it," she said.

"Doing what?"

"Explaining something because you're worried and it feels better than not knowing what will happen."

He considered the statement. "Yes. I am."

"You can keep going. I just wanted you to know that I noticed."

He reached for her hand.

It was an ordinary gesture. It had taken him years to understand that ordinary was often the point.

Foggy found Matt on a bench at the end of the hall.

"You look like you lost," he said.

"I don't like waiting."

"You never like waiting. It's probably why you have a nighttime hobby involving roof damage."

Matt smiled without opening his eyes.

"Kessler was right about the conspiracy count," he said. "A juror could reasonably doubt an agreement."

"And Malik was right about the statement."

"Yes."

"Then the jury gets to decide both. That's the part where we stop being the heroes of every story."

Matt was silent.

"You know," Foggy continued, "you cannot personally cleanse the justice system of every compromised decision."

"I know."

"You say that in a tone that suggests you're planning to try on Saturday."

"I had Monday in mind."

Foggy bumped his shoulder against Matt's.

"There he is."

Seven hours passed.

Outside, news broadcasts ran footage of the trial. Inside, lawyers checked their phones and tried not to become superstitious about the jury clock. Johnny ate two sandwiches and remained hungry. Ben fell asleep sitting upright, a geological formation at rest. Reed finally stopped trying to anticipate all twelve possible paths through the evidence.

Sue sat beside him in silence.

Near dusk, the clerk appeared and said the jury had reached a verdict.
